title: Economical–epidemiological analysis of the coffee trees rust pandemic
abstract: Coffee leaf rust is a prevalent botanical disease that causes a worldwide reduction in coffee supply and its quality, leading to immense economic losses. While several pandemic intervention policies (PIPs) for tackling this rust pandemic are commercially available, they seem to provide only partial epidemiological relief for farmers. In this work, we develop a high-resolution spatiotemporal economical–epidemiological model, extending the Susceptible-Infected-Removed model, that captures the rust pandemic’s spread in coffee tree farms and its associated economic impact. Through extensive simulations for the case of Colombia, a country that consists mostly of small-size coffee farms and is the second-largest coffee producer in the world, our results show that it is economically impractical to sustain any profit without directly tackling the rust pandemic. Furthermore, even in the hypothetical case where farmers perfectly know their farm’s epidemiological state and the weather in advance, any rust pandemic-related efforts can only amount to a limited profit of roughly 4% on investment. In the more realistic case, any rust pandemic-related efforts are expected to result in economic losses, indicating that major disturbances in the coffee market are anticipated.
summary: Coffee leaf rust is a plant disease that reduces coffee supply and quality worldwide, and the interventions on the market give farmers only partial relief. We built a detailed model of how the rust spreads across coffee farms over space and time, together with its economic impact, and simulated it for Colombia, the world's second-largest coffee producer. We found that farms cannot sustain profit without tackling the rust directly, and that even under ideal knowledge, rust-control efforts return only about 4% on investment.
key_findings: We extended the classic Susceptible-Infected-Removed epidemic model into a high-resolution economic and epidemiological model of rust spread in coffee farms.
Sustaining any profit is economically impractical without directly tackling the rust pandemic.
Even if farmers knew their farm's infection state and the weather in advance, rust-related efforts yield a profit of roughly 4% on investment.
In the more realistic case, rust-related efforts are expected to cause economic losses, pointing to major disturbances in the coffee market.
